co_slab_the_2.blurb: The Slab is the broadest chunk of rock in the Flatirons, sitting at the mouth of Fern Canyon on Boulder's south side. Its east face is a big low-angle sheet with easy, friendly lines, while the steeper north and west faces carry a dense collection of hard, pumpy sport climbs and a few trad lines, mostly from 5.11 up through 5.13. Undertow and Film Noir are the local benchmarks for the steep style. The north and west sides pick up afternoon sun, so warm days favor mornings. Small boulders sit in the trees below the wall.
co_slab_the_2.approach: Take the North Shanahan trail west and uphill; the base of the wall is around 20 to 30 minutes up. Branch left on a climbers' path through the ferns for the east face, or continue to the Fern Canyon trail and cut south over the talus for the north and west faces.

co_cob_rock.blurb: Cob Rock is a granite buttress on the south side of Boulder Canyon, part of the narrow stretch of the canyon west of town. It is mostly a trad crag, with moderate two- and three-pitch lines such as Empor and North Face Center in the 5.7+ range, plus a scattering of climbs in the 5.9 to 5.12 range and a set of boulder problems at the base, among them Face Problem and The Hug. Being on the canyon's south side, it stays shady and cool in summer and gets little winter sun. Reaching it means crossing Boulder Creek, sometimes by cable tyrolean, so keep a harness handy.
co_cob_rock.approach: Cross Boulder Creek from the highway, then climb the short trail to the base. Most Boulder Canyon crags are within about 5 to 15 minutes of the road.

co_lincoln_lake_slabs.blurb: Lincoln Lake Slabs is a high alpine cliff of granite beside the road up Mt. Blue Sky, at roughly 12,500 feet. The climbing is a mix of bolted face routes and gear lines, from low-angle moderates up to testpieces in the 5.12 and 5.13 range, with most of the grades falling between 5.9 and 5.12. Strobe Light Rodeo, Sick Puppy and Jabba are the best-known lines. Most of the rock faces north, northeast or east, so it sees sun roughly from early morning to mid-afternoon. At this altitude summer lightning storms are common, so start early and keep an eye on the sky.
co_lincoln_lake_slabs.parking_note: Small pullouts sit on the drop-off side of the road at and just beyond the corner past the top of the last cliff. Space is limited.

co_bell_buttress_main_crag.blurb: Bell Buttress is one of the larger granite walls in Boulder Canyon, and the Main Crag holds the bulk of its roped climbing. It is mainly traditional, with a handful of bolted lines, and the grades lean toward the upper end: plenty of 5.10 through 5.12, a few 5.13 sport routes, and a short list of 5.9 crack classics such as West Crack and West Face. Cosmosis and Epiphany are favorites. The wall is on the canyon's south side, so it is cool in summer and slow to warm in winter. You cross Boulder Creek to reach it, sometimes on a cable tyrolean.
co_bell_buttress_main_crag.approach: Cross Boulder Creek from the highway and follow the trail up to the base of the wall; most canyon crags are within roughly 5 to 15 minutes of the road.

co_creek_side_2.blurb: Creek Side is the biggest expanse of continuous rock in Clear Creek Canyon, a tall east-facing wall above the stream west of Golden. The stone is a mix of gneiss and schist, with some fractured sections and some very solid ones. It has a mix of older trad and mixed lines and many bolted sport routes, with grades running from 5.7 up through 5.12 and a good number of 5.8s to 5.10s. Guppy, Playin' Hooky and Black Gold are among the moderate favorites. Because it faces east it gets sun only in the morning and can feel cold and breezy the rest of the day.
co_creek_side_2.parking_note: Use the lot near Tunnel 5 on US-6, just west of the tunnel. Hop the guardrail from there to reach the creek.
co_creek_side_2.approach: From the Tunnel 5 pullout, follow the creek west for about 250 yards to reach the east side of the wall. The west side needs a rope-assisted crossing and is a more committing way in.

co_free_form_wall.blurb: Free Form Wall is one of the two main walls in Sand Gulch at Shelf Road, facing the Contest Wall across the drainage. The limestone here is mostly sport, packed into steady grades with most climbs between 5.10 and 5.12 and a big cluster of 5.11s, so it suits climbers working through that range. Freeform, Partners in Crime and Minimum Security are well-known lines. The wall stays shaded until around noon, which helps on warm days, and it sits close enough to the Sand Gulch campground to make it a convenient base.
co_free_form_wall.parking_note: Follow the gravel road through the Sand Gulch campsites to the day-use lot at the far end. Overflow parking is at the north end of the campground.

co_project_wall.blurb: Project Wall is the most visible crag in Rifle Mountain Park, a steep limestone wall that rises almost from the road at a tight bend in the canyon. Water streaks run up its overhanging face and a central cave holds some of the hardest climbing in Rifle. Nearly all of it is sport, and the grades are firmly on the hard side: mostly 5.12 through 5.14, with only a few routes below that. Apocalypse, Hang 'Em Higher and Simply Read are among the best known. Expect roadside traffic and a crowd waiting on popular lines, especially on weekends.
co_project_wall.parking_note: A small pullout below Apocalypse fits about three cars. Overflow goes at the Anti-Phil pullout just down canyon or at Ruckman Cave, with a short walk back.
co_project_wall.approach: The wall is right beside the road, a few steps from where you park.

co_dry_fork_cliff.blurb: Dry Fork Cliff is a small, little-visited cliff band reached from Lightner Creek Road west of Durango, with a climbing history that goes back decades. It is almost entirely traditional, with cracks, corners and chimneys, and the grades are friendly: most climbs fall between 5.6 and 5.9, with a few 5.10s and only one or two harder. The face looks east. It is a place for solitude rather than a destination crag, and the approach is steeper than the cliff size suggests, so expect a sweaty hike up from the road.
co_dry_fork_cliff.approach: From the drainage, a bushwhack leads up to the cliff band and takes roughly 30 to 45 minutes. An alternative is a trail that climbs the slope from the large dirt lot by the wildlife area sign.

co_primo_wall.blurb: Primo Wall is an overhanging, southeast-facing sport crag at the top of Clear Creek Canyon, west of Golden. It is home to some of the hardest climbing in the canyon, with most routes between 5.12 and 5.14 and a few easier lines to warm up on. The holds are all natural, and bolting is generally good. Public Solitude, Portrait in Flesh and Primeval are among the highlights. Patchy tree shade makes it a reasonable summer choice when other walls bake, though winter days here can feel harsh.
co_primo_wall.parking_note: Use the large pullout on the north side of US-6 just past Tunnel 6, around 11.3 miles up the canyon.
co_primo_wall.approach: Cross the creek on the tyrolean if it is rigged, then follow the trail to the cliff. Without it, drive a short way farther up the canyon, park on the south side and follow a rough trail downstream; it has some exposed scrambling.

co_sunshine_wall.blurb: Sunshine Wall is a granite wall in the Cathedral Spires area of the South Platte, west of Cynical Pinnacle. It is mainly traditional climbing on moderate-length routes, with a few bolted lines, and the grades cluster from 5.9 through 5.11 with some 5.12s. Turkey Foot Crack, Standard Route and Equinox are the lines most climbers come for. The approach follows an old road before a steep faint trail up to the base, and late-morning shadows cross the wall.
co_sunshine_wall.parking_note: A large lot serves the Cathedral Spires trailhead.
co_sunshine_wall.approach: Walk the old logging road past a switchback and across a mostly dry streambed. At a cairn, a faint trail on the right climbs steeply to the left end of the wall.

_conflicts.co_slab_the_2: parking_name: stored NCAR lot at top of Table Mesa Drive, sources say park at the Cragmoor Road dead end and take the North Shanahan trail (https://www.mountainproject.com/area/105745364/the-slab, https://www.mountainproject.com/area/109121060/fern-canyon-bouldering); aspect: stored E, but the hard sport lines are on the N and W faces, so blurb omits direction as a single face.
